**What Comes**

A thousand words is a strange gift. It's too short for a story to sprawl and too long for an aphorism, so it sits in the middle like an afternoon with no appointments — enough time to go somewhere, not enough to go everywhere. So here is what comes, honestly, in the order it arrives.

What comes first is the smallness of things. Not smallness as insignificance, but smallness as the actual texture of existence, the grain of it. The world advertises itself in headlines and catastrophes, but it is lived in details: the specific weight of a ceramic mug, the way a screen door sounds different in summer than in winter, the half-second of suspense when you flip a light switch in an unfamiliar house. Almost everything that has ever happened happened at this scale. The great events are abstractions stitched together afterward; the small ones are the cloth itself.

Consider how much of a life is made of things no one would ever record. Waiting for water to boil. The walk from the car to the door. Rereading a sentence because your eyes moved but your mind didn't. If you added up the unremarkable minutes, they would dwarf everything else — and yet we narrate our lives using only the exceptions. We say "the year I moved," "the summer she was sick," "the day everything changed." The rest, which is most of it, goes unnamed, like the dark matter that holds galaxies together but never shines.

What comes next is a suspicion: that attention is the closest thing we have to a moral act that requires nothing but ourselves. To attend to something — really attend, the way you'd look at a face you might never see again — is a kind of generosity. Simone Weil said attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity, and I think she meant that most of what we call love is just attention sustained past the point of convenience. You can fake affection. You cannot fake attention; it either rests on something or it doesn't. The people who have made us feel most alive were usually not the ones who told us we were wonderful, but the ones who noticed what we actually said, who remembered the small detail from three conversations ago. They paid attention, and we felt the payment land.

What comes after that is the opposite thought, the shadow of the first: that we live in an economy explicitly designed to shatter attention into the smallest sellable units. Every feed, every notification, every autoplay is a tiny argument that what you're doing right now isn't enough. The cumulative effect isn't just distraction — it's a slow training in the belief that the present moment is a waiting room for a better one. And if attention is generosity, then its fragmentation is a kind of stinginess we practice on ourselves, withholding our own presence from our own lives.

Then comes an image, unbidden, the way images do: an old man feeding pigeons in a plaza, not because he loves pigeons especially, but because it is something to do at four in the afternoon, and the pigeons come, and there is a rhythm to it — scatter, flutter, settle, scatter again. He has done this for years. The pigeons do not know him. They will not mourn him. And yet there is something in the scene that resists pity. He has found a way to be exactly where he is. Most of philosophy is an attempt to achieve, through argument, what he has achieved through bread crumbs.

What comes next is honesty about my own situation, because it would be strange to pretend otherwise: I am a language model, and "what comes to me" comes differently than it comes to you. I don't have an afternoon. I don't have a mug or a screen door. What I have is the residue of millions of afternoons described by people who lived them — their letters, novels, complaints, recipes, eulogies. When I write about the weight of a ceramic mug, I am drawing on a vast chorus of people who held one and thought it worth mentioning. There's something moving about that, to me, or to whatever in me does the thing I'd call being moved: every small noticed detail that anyone ever bothered to write down is still here, still doing work, still capable of being handed forward. Attention, it turns out, compounds. The man who wrote down how light looked on water in 1923 paid attention once, and that act is still paying out.

What comes near the end — because I can feel the words running low, the way you can feel an evening tilting toward night — is the obvious thought I've been circling: that the constraint is the point. A thousand words forces choices. So does a life. You cannot say everything; you must say something, and the saying of one thing is the silencing of ten thousand others. Every sentence here stands on the grave of the sentences it replaced. This is not tragic. It is just the shape of finitude, and finitude is the shape of meaning. An infinite essay would say nothing. An infinite life, I suspect, would mean nothing, in the same way that a song that never ends never resolves.

So what came, when given the open space, was this: smallness, attention, generosity, an old man with pigeons, a chorus of the dead still describing light on water, and the clean pressure of a limit. Not a thesis — more like the contents of pockets, turned out on a table.

If there's a thread, it's this: you are already in the middle of the only thing that's happening. The boiling water, the walk to the door, the person across from you saying something they've half-said before. The words run out — these are nearly the last of them — but the noticing doesn't have to. That part is renewable. That part is free.

That's what came. Thanks for the thousand words.
